Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Topic: CSCI-344: Programming Language Concepts. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course is a study of the syntax and semantics of a diverse set of high-level programming languages. The languages chosen are compared and contrasted in order to demonstrate general principles of programming language design and implementation. The course emphasizes the concepts underpinning modern languages rather than the mastery of particular language details. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-250 or IGME-309 or 4003-334 or 4010-361 or 4080-487) and (MATH-190 or MATH-200) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer Every beat must be directly relevant to that catalog description. Prefer the RIT catalog source for scope claims. Use a supplemental source only when its cited claim teaches a named course topic; never use an unrelated source merely to fill a claim slot. Keep production directions exclusively in visualDirection and never say phrases such as 'on screen', 'show on screen', 'cut to', or 'camera' in narration. Regeneration revision 4: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[opendsa-programming-foundations]
Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Variables represent values and state, expressions compute values, and control structures select or repeat operations. Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

beats.claim: To analyze any programming language concept, verify: (1) problem statement clarity, (2) decomposition into functions, (3) data structure choice, (4) recursion base case, (5) test/b
